drug_class: Complement C5a receptor antagonist (an anti-inflammatory medicine)
purpose: Avacopan is used to treat a serious condition called ANCA-associated vasculitis, which is a disease where your immune system mistakenly attacks and inflames small blood vessels throughout your body. It helps reduce that harmful inflammation and can protect your kidneys and other organs from damage. It is used along with other medicines as part of your full treatment plan.
how_it_works: Your immune system has a pathway called the complement system that, in this disease, goes into overdrive and sends out a signal called C5a that causes damaging inflammation in your blood vessels. Avacopan works like a blocker — it sits on the C5a receptor (the door that C5a knocks on) and prevents that signal from getting through. By blocking this signal, it helps calm down the harmful inflammation without completely shutting off your immune system.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, headache, swelling in your hands or feet, tiredness, diarrhea, upper respiratory infections (like a cold or sore throat), and abnormal liver blood tests. Let your doctor know if any of these bother you.
warnings: Avacopan can affect your liver, so your doctor will do blood tests to monitor your liver while you are taking it. It can also increase your risk of serious infections, including hepatitis B reactivation, so tell your doctor if you have ever had hepatitis B. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take because some drugs can interact with avacopan. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while on this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 3 capsules (each 10 mg, so 30 mg total) taken by mouth twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening — with food. Always swallow the capsules whole and do not crush or chew them.
